chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: How Hawkins and Jimmy Harrison got John Kirby into Fletcher's band
summary: Harrison secretly practiced the bass book at Kirby's house until Kirby could handle Fletcher's keys, then they feigned surprise when Fletcher gave bassist Bobby Yzaguirre notice; Kirby lifted the band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: John was in New York, and the guys used to hang out. Fletcher had a bass player was an original bass player named Ralph Escoderá. After Ralph Escoderá, there was another bass player called Bobby Vs Iguirre, Father Segueiri. He was a foreign guy. He was an excellent bass player, reading wise, but he couldn't improvise, you know, one of those things, put those extra beats in, things like that.

Well, Hawk and three or four of the other guys, Jimmy Harrison, he knew John Kirby, and they had gone around to where John was playing with a small combo, and they came and told Fletcher about him. Man, you ought to put in a man named John Kirby, plays bass. He can play tuba, and, you know, he plays upright bass. So Fletcher says, 'Well, if you guys think he's good, I'll go listen to him,' so Fletcher did, and -- funny thing about it, John was a little reluctant to come in the band at that time because he was kind of afraid of Fletcher's book, you know, because of the A natural and D natural things like that.

So Jimmy Harrison, the trombone player, was a great agitator who put -- all in fun, you know -- but this wasn't exactly fun because one -- let me tell you how they really wanted John. He would wait until the band would close Roseland at night. Jimmy Harrison was living pretty close to John Kirby. Jimmy Harrison used to take up the bass book every night and take it to John Kirby's house. All day long the next day he

would practice, go through it and everything. He would practice for about two weeks, all this kind of stuff, until he found out that he could do the job, you know, one of those things. So Fletcher said, "Well, let me know when you're ready, you know, I have to give him notice, you know. So Hawk and them were encouraging John, you know. John was always funny. He was a comical, happy go lucky guy, you know. Nothing bothered John Kirby.

So after he'd practiced (inaudible) in the book and got the things under his fingers as well. But Jimmy he would take this book back every night, though, because some nights Bobby Yzaguirre Father Segueira would say, somebody's been in my book or it down or something, said, because, like, you know --

So (inaudible) nobody said anything-- guys just looked at each other quick. So one night I happened. Fletcher gave Bobby Yzaguirre Father Segueira his notice, and he was a nice guy. So he came over, first of all, to Coleman Hawkins at intermission. He says, "Well, Hawk, I only have two more weeks in the band. I sure have enjoyed playing with you." He says, "I got my notice tonight." Hawk said, "You got your notice? I don't understand Smack." He's talking about my brother. "Why, Smack want to change you?" Man, you play, you knock me out, you know, so and so, you know. And Jimmy Harrison, the guy would take the book and take him

his book home every night, said, "I just don't understand. I just don't understand this. I can't understand. There you're playing, you're doing so and so. Man, these guys would do, you know?" (Laughter)

And the guy never knew any different. And, boy, this is what they would do. But this was the only time that they did something like that that I didn't think was fair, you know? But they wanted the guy in. This wasn't a joke. This was reality, you know, but they wanted -- Bobby was mechanical in his playing, you know what that is?
So they had a group there, but John Kirby came in that band, man, and lifted it up just like it was night and day.
Yeah, it really can make a difference.

Yes. And he was another one that looked around and could talk while he was playing. He'd play, man, was tchaw-tchaw-tchaw-tchaw, walking that bass thing. He could do things on a tuba. He was doubling when he came in. Man, he would tchaw talk, you know, behind, and he'd be playing something on the tuba, and he'd look around, wink his eye, and he'd get back in there, you know, and he'd -- he was just an asset to the group. He stayed for years with Fletcher, until he formed his own group. But John Kirby was a legend.
